hints: Think how bonding changes across Period 3 from left to right, from highly electropositive Na to electronegative non-metals.
Link bonding to structure, giant lattices have very high melting points while simple molecules are gases, liquids or low melting solids.
Remember aluminium chloride is borderline, it is ionic in the solid but becomes covalent simple molecular when heated.
For oxidation state, remember each Cl is -1, so balance the total to zero for a neutral chloride.
walkthrough:
Follow the bonding trend across the period**
Picture the metals on the left and the non-metals on the right. $\text{NaCl}$ is clearly ionic between $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$. As charge density increases, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ is polarising and borderline, accepted as ionic or covalent. By $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ and $\text{PCl}_{5}$ you have definite sharing of electrons, so covalent.

Match structure to bonding**
Ionic chlorides form giant lattices, so $\text{NaCl}$ and solid $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ are G. Covalent chlorides exist as separate small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, so $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ and $\text{PCl}_{5}$ are simple, S. $\text{PCl}_{3}$ and $\text{SCl}_{2}$ given as S fit this pattern.

Work out oxidation states quickly**
Let oxidation state of Period 3 element be x. For neutral $\text{XCl}_{n}$, $x + n(-1) = 0$, so $x = +n$. That gives $\text{NaCl}$ +1, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ +3, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ +4, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ +5, $\text{PCl}_{3}$ +3, $\text{SCl}_{2}$ +2.

Final answer: Bonding: $\text{NaCl}$ I, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ I or C, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ C, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ C.
Structure: $\text{NaCl}$ G, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ G, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ S, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ S.
Oxidation states: Na +1, Al +3, Si +4, P in $\text{PCl}_{5}$ +5, P in $\text{PCl}_{3}$ +3, S in $\text{SCl}_{2}$ +2.

hints: Ask yourself whether NaCl breaks covalent bonds in water or simply has its ions separated by water.
Recall that high oxidation state covalent chlorides like PCl5 react fully with water to give the oxoacid plus HCl.
Check balancing and remember both equations need correct state symbols for every species.
walkthrough:
See NaCl as dissolving, not reacting**
$\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ are already ions. Water just pulls the giant lattice apart and hydrates the ions. No new covalent bonds are made or broken, no HCl fumes. So write a simple dissociation: $$\text{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)}$$

See PCl5 as full hydrolysis**
$\text{PCl}_{5}$ is covalent with P in +5 state. Water attacks P, replaces every Cl with O and OH, giving phosphoric acid plus hydrochloric acid. Balance Cl first: 5 Cl need 5 HCl, then balance H and O: $$\text{PCl}_{5}\text{(s)} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}\text{(aq)} + 5\text{HCl(aq)}$$

Add every state symbol**
NaCl is solid dissolving to aqueous ions. $\text{PCl}_{5}$ is solid, water is liquid, both acid products are aqueous. Missing any state symbol loses the third mark, so check each formula.

Final answer: $\text{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)}$
$\text{PCl}_{5}\text{(s)} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}\text{(aq)} + 5\text{HCl(aq)}$ with all state symbols correct.

hints: Remember Al2Cl6 is two AlCl3 units joined together, with two Cl atoms bridging between the two Al atoms.
Think which bonds are normal shared pairs and which are dative bonds from a bridging Cl lone pair into the empty orbital on the other Al.
walkthrough:
Build the skeleton**
Imagine two $\text{Al}$ centres side by side. Two $\text{Cl}$ atoms sit between them as bridges, each bonded to both Al atoms. Each Al also has two terminal $\text{Cl}$ atoms. That gives $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Cl}_{6}$ in total.

Show normal and dative bonds**
Each terminal $\text{Al-Cl}$ is a normal covalent bond, one dot plus one cross. Each bridging Cl forms one normal bond to one Al and one dative bond to the other Al, using one of its lone pairs donated into the vacant orbital on Al. Complete every Cl with 8 electrons (3 lone pairs plus one bonding pair for terminal, 2 lone pairs plus two bonding pairs for bridging) and each Al with 8 electrons.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram of $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Cl}_{6}$ showing 2 Al bridged by 2 Cl, 4 terminal Cl, with 2 dative bonds from bridging Cl to second Al, all atoms with complete octets and correct lone pairs.

hints: Use the sign of delta H for equation 1 to decide which direction is exothermic and how added heat shifts equilibrium.
walkthrough:
Apply Le Chatelier to heat**
Equation 1 has $\Delta H_{r} = -63 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, so dimer formation to the right releases heat. Adding heat is like adding product, so the system absorbs heat by favouring the endothermic direction to the left. More $\text{AlCl}_{3}\text{(g)}$ forms and less $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Cl}_{6}\text{(g)}$ remains.
Final answer: Increase in temperature shifts equilibrium to the left, towards $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, because forward reaction is exothermic so reverse endothermic reaction is favoured.

hints: Rearrange pV = nRT to n = pV / RT and list p, V, R, T in SI units.
Convert pressure from kPa to Pa and volume from cm3 to m3 before substituting.
Once you have Mr = mass / n, compare it to the Mr values of the Period 3 chlorides in Table 2.1.
walkthrough:
Get moles from the gas equation**
You need $n = pV/RT$. Convert carefully: $$p = 323 \text{ kPa} = 3.23 \times 10^{5} \text{ Pa}$$ $$V = 250 \text{ cm}^{3} = 250 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^{3} = 2.50 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{3}$$ $$T = 500 \text{ K}, R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$ Substitute: $$n = \frac{(3.23 \times 10^{5})(2.50 \times 10^{-4})}{8.31 \times 500} = 0.0194 \text{ mol}$$

Convert mass to Mr**
Use $M_{r} = mass/n$: $$M_{r} = \frac{3.30}{0.0194} \approx 170$$ Keep 2 or 3 significant figures, 170 is fine.

Match to a Period 3 chloride**
Calculate: $\text{Si}(28.1) + 4 \times 35.5 = 170.1$. That matches exactly. $\text{PCl}_{3}$ is about 137, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ about 208, $\text{SCl}_{2}$ about 103. So the gas must be $\text{SiCl}_{4}$.

Final answer: $n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{3.23 \times 10^{5} \times 250 \times 10^{-6}}{8.31 \times 500} = 0.0194$
$M_{r} = 3.30 \div 0.0194 = 170$
Formula = $\text{SiCl}_{4}$

hints: Recall the colour of aqueous bromine and think whether a displacement reaction would change it.
Compare oxidising power of bromine and chlorine to decide if bromide can force chloride to lose electrons.
walkthrough:
Predict the observation**
Aqueous bromine is orange. If $\text{Cl}^{-}$ displaced $\text{Br}_{2}$, the orange colour would disappear. That does not happen here, so you see no change, the solution stays orange.

Explain with oxidising strength**
Displacement goes only from a stronger oxidiser to a weaker one. Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so $\text{Cl}_{2}$ can oxidise $\text{Br}^{-}$, but the reverse is impossible. $\text{Br}_{2}$ cannot take electrons from $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
Final answer: Orange solution remains, no visible reaction. $\text{Br}_{2}$ is not a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise $\text{Cl}^{-}$.

hints: Note the puzzle, SBr2 has larger Mr but is a gas, so London forces alone cannot explain why SCl2 is a liquid.
Compare the electronegativity of Cl versus Br and think how this affects the polarity of the S-X bond and the permanent dipole.
walkthrough:
Spot why Mr is misleading**
Normally a larger $M_{r}$ means stronger London dispersion forces and higher boiling point. Here $\text{SBr}_{2}$ ($M_{r} = 191.9$) should boil higher than $\text{SCl}_{2}$ ($M_{r} = 103.1$), but the opposite is true. So another force must dominate.

Bring in permanent dipoles**
Both molecules are bent and polar, so they have permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces plus London forces. Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, so the $\text{S-Cl}$ bond dipole is larger than $\text{S-Br}$. The total intermolecular attraction is therefore stronger in $\text{SCl}_{2}$, needing more energy to separate molecules, so it is a liquid while $\text{SBr}_{2}$ is a gas.

Final answer: Intermolecular forces are stronger in $\text{SCl}_{2}$ than in $\text{SBr}_{2}$ due to stronger permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces. $\text{S-Cl}$ is more polar than $\text{S-Br}$ as Cl is more electronegative than Br.

hints: Picture what particles are present in a metal, positive ions in fixed positions plus mobile electrons.
Remember to label both the cations and the delocalised electrons clearly in your diagram.
walkthrough:
Draw the metallic model**
Draw at least four circles in two rows in a regular lattice to represent $\text{Bi}$ cations. Around and between them draw many small dots or $\text{e}^{-}$ symbols to represent the mobile electrons. Do not draw molecules or shared pairs.

Label clearly**
Label the positive circles as $\text{Bi}^{n+}$ ions, cations or positive ions, and label the dots as delocalised electrons or sea of electrons. Both labels are needed for full marks.
Final answer: Diagram showing regular arrangement of $\text{Bi}^{n+}$ cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons, with labels for cations and delocalised electrons.

hints: Use the melting point clue, what type of structure melts easily with gentle heating.
Use the reaction with water clue, which type of chloride gives an acidic solution on hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Deduce structure from melting point**
$\text{BiCl}_{3}$ is a solid but melts on gentle heating. A giant ionic lattice would need very high temperature to melt. Easy melting means only weak intermolecular forces between separate molecules are broken, so structure is simple molecular.

Deduce bonding from water reaction**
Ionic chlorides like NaCl just dissolve neutrally. Vigorous reaction with water to form an acidic solution with HCl is characteristic of covalent chlorides undergoing hydrolysis. So bonding in $\text{BiCl}_{3}$ is covalent.
Final answer: Structure is simple molecular as $\text{BiCl}_{3}$ has a low melting point. Bonding is covalent as $\text{BiCl}_{3}$ is hydrolysed by water to give an acidic solution.
